children.translated_text: First Canto
With the sun fierce and the moon longed for,
with water reserves diminished by constant immersion,
delightful in the latter part of the day, with the passion of love subsided,
this summer season has arrived, O beloved.
The nights, with their darkness dispelled by the moon's rays,
houses with wonderful water-fountains here and there,
gem-studded ramparts, and cooling sandalwood paste—
in the hot season, beloved, these become sought after by people.
The fragrant palace terrace, charming,
wine stirred by the breath from a beloved's face,
song accompanied by the lute, kindling desire—
lovers enjoy these in the hot season's beautiful nights.
With their rounded hips clad in fine silk and girdles,
with breasts adorned with pearl necklaces and sandalwood,
with hair perfumed by bathing unguents,
women allay the summer heat of their lovers.
By the feet of voluptuous women, deeply reddened with lac dye,
adorned with anklets,
imitating the call of swans at every step,
the minds of people are filled with desire.
Breasts anointed with sandalwood paste,
adorned with garlands of pearls white as frost,
and hips adorned with golden girdles—
whose mind do they not fill with longing?
With perspiration rising at the joints of their limbs,
casting off their heavy garments now,
upon their breasts, these full-bosomed young women
place only a thin cloth.
By breezes born of fans wet with sandalwood water,
by the placing of pearl necklaces upon the circles of their breasts,
by the sweet sounds of the <s>vallakī</s> (lute) and <s>kākalī</s> (a musical mode)—
<s>Manmatha</s> (the god of love) is awakened today, as if from sleep.
Upon white palaces at night, the faces of women
sleeping in pleasure—the moon
having gazed upon them, surely becomes greatly agitated, and for long,
at the end of night, turns pale as if from shame.
With swirling dust clouds raised by unbearable wind,
the earth scorched by the fierce sun's heat
cannot even be looked upon by travelers
whose hearts are already burnt by the fire of separation from their beloveds.
Deer, greatly tormented by the fierce sun's heat,
their palates parched with intense thirst,
rush through the forest toward water,
having seen the sky dark as split collyrium.
With playful, smiling, sidelong glances,
graceful women, in the minds of travelers,
quickly kindle the fire of <s>Anaṅga</s> (the bodiless god of love),
just as the early evenings adorned with the beautiful moon do.
Greatly scorched by the rays of the sun,
burning on the path with heated dust,
with face cast down, moving crookedly, panting repeatedly,
a serpent sits beneath the shade of a peacock's tail.
Its vigor and effort destroyed by great thirst,
panting repeatedly with jaws widely stretched,
the lion does not strike the elephants even when close by,
its tongue lolling, the tips of its mane trembling.
With water droplets rising from their dried-up throats,
tormented by the rays of the sun,
afflicted by intense thirst, seeking water,
the elephants do not even fear the lions.
By the sun's rays like sacrificial fire,
peacocks, weary in body and spirit,
do not strike the serpent dwelling nearby,
its face nestled within the circles of their tail-feathers.
Digging in the lake with dried mud and <s>bhadramustā</s> (a type of grass),
with long rows of snouts,
greatly scorched by the rays of the sun,
a herd of boars seems to burrow into the earth.
Scorched by the sun with its exceedingly sharp garland of rays,
from the lake with its muddy water,
a frog leaps out and sits
beneath the umbrella-like hood of a thirsty serpent.
With all the networks of lotus stalks pulled up,
its fish perished, its <s>sārasa</s> (cranes) fled in haste,
by elephants pressing together upon one another,
the lake is made thick with churned-up mud.
Its crest-gem's luster broken by the sun's radiance,
the wind licked by its two flickering tongues,
tormented by the heat of its own venom, fire, and the sun, the serpent,
overcome by thirst, does not strike the frog colony.
With mouths covered in foamy saliva,
with blood-red tongues protruding, faces upturned,
overcome by thirst, emerging from mountain caves,
a herd of buffalo gazes toward water.
With sprouting grasses withered by the exceedingly fierce heat of the wildfire,
with dried leaves scattered by the force of harsh winds,
with water diminished all around by the sun's heat,
the forest regions, when beheld, inspire great fear.
Flocks of birds pant upon trees with fallen leaves,
troops of monkeys, exhausted, seek the mountain groves,
herds of <s>gavaya</s> (wild oxen) wander everywhere seeking water,
and the <s>śarabha</s> (a mythical eight-legged beast) draws water straight up from wells.
With a blaze bright as blossoming <s>kusumbha</s> (safflower) and clear vermilion,
swiftly intensified by the force of powerful winds,
entangling the creepers and treetops along the banks,
the wildfire has burnt the earth in every direction.
Intensified by wind, it blazes in the caverns of mountains,
it crackles with sharp sounds in the dry bamboo groves,
it spreads through the grass, gaining strength in an instant,
the forest fire, clinging to the edges, torments the herds of deer.
Seeming to multiply in the forests of <s>śālmalī</s> (silk-cotton trees),
blazing gold-bright in the hollows of trees,
leaping up to tall trees with their branches of withered leaves,
the fire, driven by wind, roams everywhere through the forest.
Elephants, wild oxen, and lions, their bodies scorched by fire,
come together like friends, abandoning their natural enmity;
swiftly emerging from the thicket, distressed by the wildfire,
they enter the broad sandy banks of the river.
With waters filled with lotus groves, delightful with pink depths,
with pleasant sprinklings of cool water, with moonbeams and garlands to enjoy,
may your summer, O beloved, pass in the company of beautiful women,
on the palace rooftop at night, with sweet songs and comfort.
Second Canto
With clouds like rutting elephants bearing fine spray,
with lightning for its banners and thunder for its drums,
the rainy season has arrived like a king, resplendent in its glory,
dear to those who love, O beloved.
With clouds having the hue of deep blue lotus petals,
some resembling heaps of freshly split collyrium,
some having the luster of the breasts of women heavy with child,
the sky is covered with clouds on all sides.
Implored by flocks of thirsty <s>cātaka</s> (rain-birds),
hanging heavy with their burden of water,
the rain clouds move slowly, pouring rain in many streams,
their sound pleasing to the ear and mind.
The rain clouds, with thunder for their drums,
bearing <s>Indra</s>'s bow (the rainbow) strung with lightning,
with their fierce arrows of sharp, falling rain-drops,
strike forcefully at the hearts of travelers.
Covered with grass shoots resembling split emeralds,
spread with the risen leaves of <s>kandalī</s> (plantain),
adorned with gems other than white—
the earth shines like a beautiful woman, with <s>indragopaka</s> (scarlet insects) as her jewels.
Always delightful, eager for the festival of their cries,
adorned with their widely spread, splendid tail-feathers,
agitated by the frenzy of embracing and kissing,
the flock of peacocks has begun its dance today.
Toppling the trees along their banks on all sides,
with swollen, turbid waters of great force,
like thoroughly wicked women who have lost all sense of propriety,
the rivers rush swiftly toward the ocean.
With tufts of grass sprouting tender shoots,
dotted with dark ones nibbled by the mouths of does,
the <s>Vindhya</s> forests captivate the mind,
adorned by trees putting forth new leaves.
With deer all around, their beautiful faces adorned by restless lotus-petal eyes,
newly startled,
the sandy woodland
stirs longing in the heart.
Even in nights made pitch dark
by the clouds thundering loudly and incessantly,
with lightning flashes revealing the path before them,
women go forth to meet their lovers, driven by passion.
By clouds with deep, terrifying rumbles,
and by lightning that greatly agitates their hearts,
women embrace their lovers on the bed without pause,
even those against whom they had borne a grievance.
With tears like drops of water from lotus-like eyes,
upon their beautiful <s>bimba</s>-fruit-red lower lips,
having cast off garlands, ornaments, and unguents,
the wives of travelers stand bereft of hope.
Pale, carrying bits of insects, grass,
creeping in winding paths like a serpent,
watched with alarm by the frog colonies,
the fresh water flows toward the lowlands.
Leaving eagerly the lotus pond now bereft of leaves and flowers,
bees with their sounds pleasing to the ear
fall, deluded, upon the tail-fan circles
of the dancing peacocks, mistaking them for fresh blue lotuses.
Of forest elephants, trumpeting again and again
in excitement at the sound of fresh rain clouds,
the temples, lustrous as spotless blue lotuses,
are covered with swarms of bees drawn to their ichor.
With rocks kissed by clouds bright as white lotuses,
surrounded on all sides by waterfalls,
teeming with peacocks that have begun their dance,
the mountains inspire a feeling of longing.
Shaking the groves of <s>kadamba</s>, <s>sarja</s>, <s>arjuna</s>, and <s>ketakī</s>,
fragrant with their blossoms,
cooled by contact with clouds bearing fine spray,
the breeze—whom does it not fill with longing?
With tresses hanging down to the slopes of their hips,
with fragrant flowers worn as ear-ornaments,
with breasts like necklaces and faces accompanied by wine,
women arouse passion in their lovers.
They flow, they pour, they roar, they shine,
they spread out, they dance, they take shelter —
the rivers, the clouds, the intoxicated elephants, the forest edges,
those bereft of their beloveds, the peacocks, and the frogs.
Adorned with streaks of lightning and rainbows,
the rain-clouds hanging heavy with their burden of water,
and women radiant with girdle-gems and earrings —
both steal the hearts of travelers at once.
Garlands woven from the fresh filaments of <s>kadamba</s> and <s>ketakī</s> flowers
women now wear upon their heads,
and at the sides of their ears, with the flower-clusters of the <s>kubuja</s> tree,
[they wear] ear-ornaments fashioned according to their fancy.
Their limbs anointed with dark <s>aguru</s> (aloe) paste and excellent sandalwood,
their tresses made fragrant with flower-ornaments,
hearing the rumble of the rain-clouds at dusk, quickly
the women enter the bedchamber from the house of the elders.
With rain-clouds dark as blue lotus petals, towering, bowed with water,
gently swaying, stirred by the soft wind,
as if the hearts are stolen by the clouds bearing <s>Indra</s>'s bow (the rainbow) —
[such is the plight] of the wives of traveling men, distressed by separation from them.
As if delighted with <s>kadamba</s> trees whose flowers have opened all around,
as if dancing with trees whose branches sway in the wind,
as if laughing with the needle-like [blossoms] of the <s>ketakī</s> —
the forest edge, its heat destroyed by the sprinkling of fresh waters [rejoices].
A garland of <s>bakula</s> blossoms on the head, combined with <s>mālatī</s> (jasmine)
and buds of <s>yūthikā</s> (wild jasmine) with their fresh flowers blossoming,
an ear-ornament of fresh blooming <s>kadamba</s> for the young women —
this season arranges [all this], like a lover, with the mass of rain-clouds.
Women bear [upon] their excellent, uplifted breast-tips a string of pearls,
fine white silk garments upon their extended hip-globes,
a line of body-hair risen from the sprinkling of fresh water-drops,
and upon their waist-regions with graceful folds of skin.
Bearing coolness from the contact of fresh water-drops,
a dancer for the trees bowing under the weight of blossoms,
producing a lovely fragrance from the pollen of <s>ketakī</s> flowers —
the wind carries away the hearts of those whose beloveds are far away.
'This lofty one, bowed with the burden of water, is our refuge' —
saying thus, the clouds, bowed with water, with their water-showers,
seem to soothe the <s>Vindhya</s> mountain, whose heat was generated
by the exceedingly fierce flames of the summer fire.
Delightful with manifold charms, stealing the hearts of lovers,
the companion of trees, creepers, and vines — unchanging,
this rainy season, the very life-breath of living beings —
may it bestow upon you blessings and grant your wishes!
Third Canto
With garments white as <s>kāśa</s> grass, with a face lovely as a full-blown lotus,
charming with the sound of anklet-bells [like] the cry of excited geese,
with a graceful body-stalk bending [like] ripening rice —
autumn has arrived, beautiful in form like a lovely new bride.
The earth [is made white] by <s>kāśa</s> grass, the nights by the cool-rayed moon,
the waters of rivers by geese, the lakes by white water-lilies,
the forest edges by <s>saptacchada</s> (seven-leaved) trees bowing under the burden of flowers,
and the groves by <s>mālatī</s> (jasmine) — all made white.
With flashing, lovely <s>śapharī</s> fish [moving like] girdle-strings,
with rows of white birds stationed at the edges [like] pearl necklaces,
the rivers, with their wide sandy banks [like] broad hip-globes,
flow gently now — like proud young women in their prime.
The sky in places, with clouds white as silver, conch, and lotus-fiber,
having shed their water, gone away in hundreds through lightness,
moving with the speed of the wind, is seen
like a king being fanned with hundreds of <s>cāmara</s> (fly-whisks).
The sky [is] lovely with the beauty of broken heaps of collyrium,
and the earth is reddened by the pollen of <s>bandhūka</s> flowers,
and the embankments are covered with ripening plantains —

children.text: protkaṇṭhayanti na mano bhuvi kasya yūnaḥ
children.translated_text: whose mind among young men on earth is not filled with longing?
With its graceful topmost branches stirred by the gentle breeze,
with tender new leaves [softened] by the profusion of emerging blossoms,
with its honey-flow sipped by intoxicated bees —
whose heart does the <s>Kovidāra</s> (Bauhinia) tree not rend asunder?
Bearing the finest ornament of the host of stars,
her moon-face released from the covering of clouds,
wearing a spotless garment of moonlight — the night
grows day by day, like a young maiden coming of age.
With garlands of waves disturbed by <s>kāraṇḍava</s> ducks,
with shores crowded by flocks of <s>kādamba</s> geese and <s>sārasa</s> cranes,
the rivers, reddened by the pollen of lotuses,
produce delight in people everywhere with the cries of geese.
A festival for the eyes, with garlands of rays that steal the heart,
refreshing, showering cool dew-drop rain —
[yet] the moon burns all the more the bodies of women
wounded by the arrows of the poison of separation from their husbands.
Shaking the nets of rice plants bowed under the weight of grain,
making the great trees dance, bowed with blossoms,
agitating the lotus-pool with its forest of full-blown lotuses —
the wind forcibly disturbs the mind of the slender-bodied one [left behind].
Adorned with pairs of excited geese,
decorated with clear, full-blown lotuses and blue water-lilies,
with garlands of waves arising in the gentle morning breeze —
the lakes suddenly fill the heart with longing.
The bow of <s>Indra</s> (the rainbow) has vanished from the bellies of the clouds;
lightning no longer flashes as a banner in the sky;
the cranes do not sweep the sky with the wind of their wings;
the peacocks gaze no more with upturned faces at the heavens.
Abandoning the peacocks, [now] devoid of [their] dance-performances,
<s>Madana</s> (the god of Love) approaches the geese, sweet in their song;
leaving the <s>kadamba</s>, <s>kuṭaja</s>, <s>arjuna</s>, <s>sarja</s>, and <s>nīpa</s> trees,
the splendor of blossoming has come to the <s>saptacchada</s> (Alstonia).
Enchanting with the fragrance of <s>śephālikā</s> (night-jasmine) blossoms,
resounding with the calls of flocks of birds resting at ease,
with blue lotuses [resembling] the eyes of does stationed at their borders —
the groves fill with longing the minds of men.
Continually shaking the <s>kahlāra</s> lotuses, day-lotuses, and night-lilies,
becoming exceedingly cool from contact with them,
the wind at dawn fills one with longing intensely,
shaking off the dew-drops clinging to the surfaces of leaves.
With fields covered by the abundance of ripened rice,
adorned with large herds of cattle resting at ease,
resounding with geese and flocks of <s>sārasa</s> cranes —
the boundaries between fields produce delight in men.
The graceful gait of women is surpassed by geese,
the moon-radiance of [their] faces by fully-opened lotuses,
their intoxicated eyes by blue water-lilies,
and their lovely arch of brows by slender waves.
The dark creepers, their tendrils bowing under the weight of blossoms,
steal the beauty of women's arms adorned with ornaments;
and the fresh <s>mālatī</s> (jasmine), lovely with <s>kaṅkeli</s> blossoms,
[steals] the moon-radiance of their clear smiles revealing their teeth.
Women fill their hair — drawn back, dense, dark-blue, with curled ends —
with fresh <s>mālatī</s> (jasmine) flowers,
and in their ears, upon excellent golden earrings,
they place various blue water-lilies.
With pearl-necklaces and sandal-paste [they adorn] the circles of their breasts,
the broad expanse of their hips with girdle-strings,
and their lotus-feet with tinkling anklet-crests —
women, with joyful hearts, now adorn themselves.
Of the lakes — studded with open white water-lilies, inhabited by royal geese,
decorated with waters shining like emerald gems —
the sky, cloudless, strewn with moon and stars,
bears their beauty in exceedingly splendid form.
In autumn the winds blow cool from contact with water-lilies,
the directions are lovely, free of masses of clouds,
the waters are freed from turbidity, the earth's mud has dried,
the sky [bears] a moon of pure rays and is variegated with stars.
With lotus-hands that are lovely, holding the hands of their beloveds,
with faces that surpass the moon — some other young women
mostly go to their homes fragrant with arranged flowers,
having abandoned the passion for song, impelled by intense desire.
Delighting in the pleasures of lovemaking, accompanied by good friends,
they freely display the sport of the Unequal-arrowed One (<s>Kāma</s>);
with incomparable lip-rouge, in the middle of the night, for amusement,
the young beautiful women in autumn display their delights.
Pressed by the rays of the sun at dawn,
the lotus — [brilliant] like the face of a choice young woman — now opens;
and the night-lily too closes when the moon-disc sets —
as if [mimicking] the smiles of young wives when their beloveds are away.
Seeing the beauty of dark eyes in the blue water-lilies,
the tinkling of golden girdles in the calls of intoxicated geese,
the lovely radiance of [their] lips in the <s>bandhujīva</s> (midday) flower — of their beloveds —
the traveler now weeps, his mind bewildered.
Leaving behind the moon-radiance on the faces of women,
and the desirable goose-song in [their] jeweled anklets,
and the <s>bandhūka</s>-glow on [their] enchanting lips —
the beauty of autumn's arrival goes away to some [unknown] place.
With a face of fully-opened lotuses, eyes of blossoming blue water-lilies,
wearing white garments [like] fresh <s>kāśa</s> grass in bloom,
with the lovely radiance of water-lilies — like a woman in the frenzy of love — this
autumn — may it bestow upon your hearts the foremost joy!
Fourth Canto
Lovely with new shoots and crops emerging,
with <s>lodhra</s> trees in full bloom, with rice ripened,
with lotuses vanished, with frost falling —
the early winter season has arrived.
With charming [necklaces] pale as sandalwood-paste,
and strings of pearls white as frost, <s>kunda</s> (jasmine), and the moon —
the breast-circles of proud women
with beautiful breasts are [no longer] adorned [with these].
On the pairs of arms of lovely women,
bracelets and armlets do not find their place;
nor does new silk upon their rounded hips,
nor thin garments upon their full breasts.
With girdle-chains brilliant with golden gems,
women do not adorn their hips,
nor with anklets that echo the sound of swans
their lotus-feet, which possess the beauty of lotuses.
Their limbs anointed with <s>kālīyaka</s> (dark sandalwood),
their lotus-faces bearing ornamental leaf-designs,
their hair perfumed with dark <s>aguru</s> (aloe-wood) incense —
women prepare themselves for the festival of love.
Young women, whose faces are pale and wan from the fatigue of love-sport,
having attained the arising of joy,
do not laugh aloud, but looking upon
their lower lips, bitten at the tip of the teeth and pressed hard.
Having reached the beauty of full breasts, chests, and bosoms,
and distressed from pressing them,
by dewdrops clinging to the tips of grass and falling —
the cold season cries out, as it were, at dawn.
Filled with abundant ripened rice,
adorned with herds of female deer,
resounding with the charming calls of <s>krauñca</s> (curlew) birds —
the border-lands stir longing in the heart.
Graced by fully-bloomed blue lotuses,
adorned by intoxicating <s>kadamba</s> trees,
with clear and pleasantly cool waters —
the lakes captivate the minds of men.
Seeing the road completely devoid of water,
women carrying [in their thoughts] their husbands wearied by travel abroad,
gazing with deer-like eyes —
seem to awaken their heart's desires.
The <s>priyangu</s> (beauty-berry) creeper, ripening,
constantly shaken by frost-born cold winds,
O beloved, separated from its dear one —
turns pale like a languishing woman.
With mouth fragrant from the sweet scent of flower-wine,
body perfumed by the wind of exhaled breaths,
sleeping entwined limb upon limb with one another —
people lie, pierced by the passion of love.
By lips bearing wound-marks of teeth-bites,
and by breasts scratched by fingertips —
the merciless enjoyment of love is proclaimed
of young women in the freshness of youth.
One woman, mirror in hand, adorns
her lotus-face in the early morning sun,
and pulling down her lower lip, whose essence was drunk by her beloved,
examines it, bitten at the tip of his teeth.
Another, her body exhausted by the fatigue of abundant love-sport,
her lotus-eyes reddened by staying awake all night,
with disheveled mass of hair charmingly falling about her drooping shoulders —
falls asleep, warmed by the gentle rays of the sun.
Having removed from their heads the wilted garlands that bore lovely fragrance when worn,
their thick dark tresses [hanging loose],
their body-stalks bent by the weight of full, uplifted breasts —
other young women arrange their hair.
Another, seeing her body enjoyed by her beloved,
joyful, with beautifully fashioned lip-charm,
puts on her bodice, her limbs marked with nail-scratches,
with curling dark locks hanging down, her eyes half-closed.
Others, exhausted for a long time by the exertion of love-sport,
their body-stalks made slack,
the tips of their breasts bristling with <s>pulaka</s> (horripilation) —
beautiful women apply their body-oil.
Lovely in many ways, captivating the hearts of women,
with village borders crowded with abundant ripened rice,
with fallen dew, celebrated by the calls of <s>krauñca</s> (curlew) birds —

children.text: pradiśatu himayuktaḥ kāla eṣaḥ sukhaṃ vaḥ
children.translated_text: may this season accompanied by frost bestow happiness upon you!
Fifth Canto.
The earth covered with grown rice and sugarcane fields,
here and there graced by the sounds of abiding <s>krauñca</s> birds,
fully delightful for passion, beloved to women —
O beautiful-thighed one, hear of the season called <s>Śiśira</s> (the cold season).
The interior of houses with windows shut,
fire, the rays of the sun,
heavy garments, and women in their youth —
in this season, these come to be enjoyed by people.
Not sandalwood cool as moonbeams,
not the terrace-top pure as the autumn moon,
not breezes cold with dense frost —
none of these delight the hearts of people now.
Cold from the fall of masses of frost,
further chilled by the rays of the moon,
adorned with pale clusters of stars —
the nights are not fit to be enjoyed by people.
Having taken betel, unguents, and garlands,
their lotus-faces fragrant with flower-wine,
bodies scented liberally with dark <s>aguru</s> (aloe-wood) incense —
eager women enter the bedchamber.
Having seen their husbands — who had committed many offenses and been much scolded,
trembling, their minds stunned with apprehension —
now desirous of love-sport,
the women, intoxicated, forgot their offenses.
By passionate youths, mercilessly,
through the long nights, delighted for long,
their breasts moving slowly, wearied by exertion —
at night's end, young women wander languidly.
Their breasts pressed by lovely bodices,
their chests adorned with colored silk,
flowers placed within their tresses —
women seem to adorn the approach of winter.
With breasts tawny from saffron-paste,
delightfully warm with the heat of fresh youth —
embraced tightly by lovely women,
lovers sleep, disregarding the cold.
Fragrant-breathed, causing lotuses to tremble,
enchanting, awakening love and passion,
at night, joyful women together with their lovers
drink the finest wine, which is intoxicating.
One woman at dawn, her intoxication and passion having faded,
the tips of her breasts pressed close by her husband's embrace,
looking upon her own body enjoyed by her dearest beloved —
leaves her sleeping-garment for another, laughing.
Bearing her mass of hair, fragrant with dark <s>aguru</s> incense,
its flower-garland fallen, its ends curled —
the heavy-hipped, deep-naveled, slender-waisted woman
leaves her bed at dawn, another beauty of charming splendor.
With face-orbs [glowing] like golden lotuses, with beautifully red lower lips,
with eyes pink at the corners resting against the temples,
at dawn, with hair clinging to their shoulders —
women stand in the midst of their homes today like <s>Śrī</s> (the goddess of beauty) herself.
Afflicted by the weight of their broad hips, their waists slightly bowed,
walking slowly, slowly, from the weariness of their breast-burden,
swiftly casting off the nightly attire of love-sport —
other young women put on garments suitable for the day.
Looking upon the tips of their breasts marked with nail-prints,
touching their bud-like lower lips bitten by teeth,
young women, delighting in the attire of desired love-sport,
adorn their faces at the time of sunrise.
Abundant in preparations of molasses, delightful with sweet rice and sugarcane,
filled with vigorous love-sport and aroused passion,
a cause of mental torment for those separated from their dear ones —
may this cold season be ever for your welfare!
Sixth Canto [Description of Spring].
With the sharp arrows of fully-blossomed mango shoots,
with the bowstring of sporting rows of bees,
to pierce the minds of those devoted to love-sport —
the warrior Spring has arrived, O beloved!
Trees are in flower, waters bear lotuses,
women are filled with desire, the breeze is fragrant,
evenings are pleasant, and days are delightful —
everything, O beloved, is more charming in spring.
With hair slightly cooled by dew,
and beautifully perfumed with <s>campaka</s> blossoms,
in the springtime, women adorn
their breasts with garlands and enchanting flowers.
To the waters of ponds, to jeweled girdles,
to moonbeams, to the company of lovely women,
to mango trees laden with blossoms —
spring bestows loveliness.
With silk dyed red with safflower,
the hips of lovely women [are adorned],
with thin garments golden-hued with saffron —
their breasts are ornamented.
Fresh <s>karṇikāra</s> blossoms [are fitting] for the ears,
<s>aśoka</s> [blossoms] for the moving dark locks,
and the full-blown <s>mallikā</s> (jasmine) flower —
these attain beauty upon the women.
On breasts, necklaces moist with white sandalwood;
on arms, bracelets and armlets find their place;
upon the hips of broad-hipped women
whose minds are tormented by <s>Anaṅga</s> (the bodiless god of love) — girdles.
On the leaf-painted faces of lovely women,
faces resembling golden lotuses,
lovely with pearls set among gems —
beads of perspiration spread.
Sighing, loosening their garment-ties,
their limbs agitated by <s>Kandarpa</s> (the god of love),
now that their beloveds are near —
the women become most eager.
Thin, pale, languid with intoxication,
given to frequent yawning,
the limbs of women —
<s>Anaṅga</s> (the bodiless Cupid) makes them quiver with loveliness.
People long for the shade of trees,
at night they desire the rays of the moon,
they go to the terrace to sleep in pleasant coolness,
and embrace their beloved tightly for her coolness.
Restless in the languid intoxicated eyes,
pale on the cheeks, firm on the breasts,
deep in the waist, full on the hips —
<s>Anaṅga</s> (the god of love) is manifested in many ways in women today.
Limbs languid with the grace of drowsiness,
words somewhat slurred with intoxication,
and glances made sidelong by the play of brows —
<s>Kāma</s> (the god of love) has wrought these in the company of women.
On fair breasts, by lovely women,
smeared with <s>priyangu</s>, <s>kālīyaka</s>, and saffron —
sandalwood paste is applied by the women
languid with intoxication and infused with musk (<s>mṛganābhi</s>).
Swiftly discarding heavy garments,
people don thin ones dyed with lac (<s>lākṣā</s>) resin,
perfumed with fragrant dark aloe-wood (<s>kālāguru</s>) incense,
[their] limbs languid with the intoxication of desire (<s>kāma</s>).
The male cuckoo (<s>puṃskokila</s>), intoxicated by the wine of mango sap,
kisses his beloved, thrilled with passion;
the bee, buzzing, resting upon a lotus,
makes sweet flattery to his beloved.
The mango trees, bowed down with clusters of copper-red new shoots,
their beautiful branches in bloom,
shaken by the wind, make
the minds of women restless with desire.
Copper-red from the root like coral,
bearing masses of flowers along with their shoots,
the <s>aśoka</s> trees make the hearts of those in the bloom of youth sorrowful,
when gazed upon by them.
With beautiful flowers kissed by intoxicated bees,
with soft new shoots bending in the gentle breeze,
the creepers newly released by the <s>bālā</s> [trees], when beheld,
suddenly arouse eagerness in the hearts of lovers.
Of the <s>kurabaka</s> flower-clusters that have recently appeared,
possessing the radiance of beloved women's faces — their supreme beauty —
having seen [them], what sensitive person's heart would not be
tormented by the falling of <s>Kandarpa</s>'s (the god of love's) arrows?
With <s>kiṃśuka</s> (flame-of-the-forest) groves everywhere, bowed with blossoms,
shaken by winds [and glowing] like blazing fire,
this earth, instantly adorned by the spring season,
shines like a new bride wearing a red garment.
Has it not already been pierced by <s>kiṃśuka</s> flowers, bright as a parrot's beak?
Has it not already been burned by <s>karṇikāra</s> blossoms?
Yet this cuckoo, with his sweet calls,
again strikes the hearts of young men already fixed upon beautiful-faced women.
By male cuckoos with melodious voices, seized with delight,
by buzzing bees uttering intoxicated notes,
the hearts of young brides — bashful and modest — are in an instant
made agitated, even in [their] family homes.
Shaking the flowering branches of mango trees,
spreading the cuckoo's song in all directions,
the wind blows, stealing the hearts of men,
delightful in spring, with the departure of the fall of frost.
With <s>kunda</s> (jasmine) flowers — white as the laughter of a playful bride —
the illuminated pleasure-gardens are enchanting;
they steal the heart even of a sage free from passion,
how much more the minds of young men, stained with desire!
With trailing golden girdles, necklaces clinging to their breasts,
their bodily grace made languid by the pride of <s>Kandarpa</s> (Cupid),
in the month of <s>Madhu</s> (spring), with the sounds of sweet cuckoos and bees,
women forcibly steal the hearts of men.
Adorned with trees bearing various delightful blossoms,
their mountain-slopes resounding with the joyful cries of various birds,
their rock-surfaces wound about with networks of mountain-herbs,
seeing the mountains, all people are filled with delight.
He closes his eyes, he weeps, he is overcome with sorrow,
he blocks his nose with his hand, he cries out aloud —
the traveler, his mind afflicted by separation from his beloved,
upon seeing the flowering mango trees.
With the calls of intoxicated bees and cuckoos,
with flowering mangoes and <s>karṇikāra</s> trees, [the month is] lovely;
like sharp arrows, it pierces the minds of proud women,
the flower-month (<s>kusumamāsa</s>), for the kindling of <s>Manmatha</s> (the god of love).
The flowering mango trees, releasing heaps of blossoms
with the splendor of beautiful gold, shaken by a gentle wind —
gazing directly upon them, even the emaciated traveler on the road
falls into a swoon from the blows of <s>Madana</s>'s (Cupid's) arrows.
With the cuckoo's delightful, melodious songs [mocking] sweet speech,
with the radiance of <s>kunda</s> (jasmine) blossoms [mocking] the rays of smiling teeth,
with sprouts red as coral [mocking] the beauty of tender hand-shoots,
spring now mocks the women of desire.
With faces [glowing] like golden lotuses, cheeks pale [with longing],
with necklaces resting above [their breasts], breast-tips moist with sandal-paste,
with glances full of coquetry born of intoxication, women
desire even the greatest sages, bowed by the weight of their breasts, [those sages being] tranquil.
The face-lotus is fragrant with spring-honey, the eyes are copper-red like <s>lodhra</s> [blossoms],
the mass of hair, filled with fresh <s>kurabaka</s> flowers, is charming,
the pair of breasts is heavy, the hips [are round] as well —
what of women's [charms] is not now an instrument of <s>Manmatha</s> (the god of love)?
The hearts of proud women are shaken
by winds perfumed by full-blown mango blossoms,
by the calls of the intoxicated cuckoo,
and by the pleasing song-sounds of the bee.
The evening hour, lovely with the bright moon's radiance,
the call of the male cuckoo, the fragrant wind,
the buzzing of swarms of intoxicated bees, the drinking of wine at night —
all this is an elixir for the Flower-weaponed One (<s>Kusumāyudha</s>, i.e., <s>Kāma</s>).
With lips fashioned like red <s>aśoka</s> [blossoms], sweet — [his] voice the sound of intoxicated bees,
with a row of teeth pure-white as a <s>kunda</s>-flower garland, with a face [radiant] as a fully-bloomed lotus,
with a breeze gentle and fragrant with the scent of mango blossoms — the preceptor in the initiation of <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic sentiment) —

children.text: kalpāntaṃ madanapriyo diśatu vaḥ puṣpāgamo maṅgalam
children.translated_text: may the arrival of flowers (<s>puṣpāgama</s>), dear to <s>Madana</s> (Cupid), bestow auspiciousness upon you until the end of the <s>kalpa</s> (cosmic age)!
Pierced by the <s>Malaya</s> mountain breeze, delightful with the cuckoo's song,
having obtained a continuous stream of fragrance from the showering of sweet nectar,
surrounded on all sides by swarms of diverse bees —
may spring, the most excellent of seasons, bring you happiness!
The mango blossom-cluster is his lovely arrow, the beautiful <s>kiṃśuka</s> is his bow,

children.text: jyā yasyālikulaṃ kalaṅkarahitaṃ chattraṃ sitāṃśuḥ sitam
children.translated_text: the string of bees is his bowstring, the spotless white moon is his white parasol,
the intoxicated elephant is the <s>Malaya</s> wind, the cuckoo is his herald — the conqueror of the world!
May that <s>Manmatha</s> (Cupid), accompanied by spring, abundantly bestow blessings upon you!
